analysis.one_liner: Strengthens consumers' rights to fix credit report errors and get free credit scores.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2017, got a single Senate Banking Committee hearing in October, and died in committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Fair Credit Reporting Act to make it easier for people to dispute and fix errors in their credit reports. It would require credit bureaus to pass consumers' documentation to the companies reporting disputed information, require the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau to write rules ensuring report accuracy, and give consumers free credit scores and free credit report copies after being denied credit or offered worse terms. It would also let parents block credit files for children under 16 to prevent identity theft, allow courts to order bureaus to comply with the law, and direct a government study of a public credit reporting alternative.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with errors on their credit reports, who currently bear the burden of fixing mistakes that can cost them loans, jobs, and housing; people denied credit or offered worse terms, who would get free copies of the reports used against them; anyone requesting a free annual credit report, who would also get a free credit score; and families with young children, who could block credit files to prevent identity theft.

how_it_helps.text: Requires credit bureaus to forward all documentation a consumer submits with a dispute to the company that reported the information, and requires that company to actually review and consider it [S3]
Lets courts order credit bureaus to comply with the law and lets the FTC pursue negligent and willful violations, not just knowing ones, giving consumers more recourse when reports are wrong [S2]
Requires a free credit score on request alongside the free annual credit report, and free credit report copies for anyone denied credit or offered worse terms because of a report [S2]
Lets parents and guardians of children under 16 place a block on the child's credit file so no one can access it or add information, protecting kids from identity theft [S3]
Directs the Government Accountability Office to study whether a government-run consumer credit reporting system is feasible, in effect examining alternatives to the three private bureaus [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Consumer credit reporting agencies (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion and others), which would face stricter accuracy rules, public dispute reporting, registration, greater litigation exposure, and the prospect of a government-run alternative being studied; plus banks, lenders, and debt collectors that furnish information, which would have to review consumer documentation in disputes and face suits over negligence.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus and lenders that report data

drawbacks.text: Agencies could charge a fee to create or unblock a child's credit file, so parents would bear a cost to use the child identity-theft protection, though fee exemptions for fraud victims would be possible [S3]
Costs and fees can be awarded to the prevailing party in injunction suits, which could expose consumers to paying a bureau's legal fees if a case fails [S3]
Stricter matching and documentation requirements would raise compliance costs for bureaus and lenders, costs that could be passed to consumers through higher prices or fees

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefits are substantial and direct: credit report errors are common and hard to fix under current law, and the bill shifts the burden toward the bureaus and data furnishers. The main costs fall on the credit reporting industry and lenders, with some possible pass-through to consumers, and the child-file fee is a real but modest flaw. The bill would also create a public record of dispute volumes and commission a study of a public alternative, which the private bureaus opposed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, got one hearing, and was never brought up for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Brian Schatz introduced the bill on September 11, 2017, joined by five other senators [S1]
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee [S5]
The committee held a hearing on the bill on October 17, 2017, printing the hearings as S.Hrg. 115-132 [S5]
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee vote or floor vote and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer reporting agencies and the banks and collectors that furnish credit data, which avoid stricter accuracy rules, litigation exposure, and a study of a public alternative.

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate

for.name: Sens. Jeff Merkley, Claire McCaskill, and Richard Blumenthal
for.role: U.S. Senators from Oregon, Missouri, and Connecticut

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired held one hearing on the bill but never brought it to a committee vote, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sanders; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled Senate Banking Committee took no vote.

industries.industry: Consumer credit reporting agencies (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion)
industries.note: The bill would require accuracy rules from the CFPB, free scores, free report copies after adverse decisions, public registration, documented dispute handling, and a GAO study of a government-run alternative. Each of these reduces the bureaus' discretion and profits while directly serving consumers who dispute errors.

industries.industry: Banks, lenders, and debt collectors that furnish credit data
industries.note: Furnishers would have to review all documentation consumers submit with disputes and could face FTC action and lawsuits over negligent or willful inaccuracies, raising compliance and litigation costs.
